gist: Customer orders a children's bear-face sausage and, asked which meat it is made of, insists it is made of bear, taking the product name literally.

characters.looks: ordinary adult shopper, puzzled face, shopping basket
butcher in white apron and cap behind counter

wordplay.explanation: 'Bärchenwurst' is a brand-like name for kids' sausage with a bear face (made of pork or turkey); the customer reads it literally as sausage made of bears.

cultureRefs: Bärchenwurst: German children's cold-cut sausage with a bear face printed on each slice

ru.note: Replace with a local kids' product whose name sounds like an animal ingredient.

en.note: Swap for a familiar product with an animal name, e.g. animal-shaped kids' sausage or 'teddy' ham.

gist: Not a joke: a new employee asks a forum for office-appropriate jokes to tell at the weekly team meeting.

characters.looks: young office worker, nervous smile, laptop

gist: Chuck Norris fact: after drinking he gets no hangover, instead the hangover is had by him, using a word that means both hangover and tomcat.

characters.looks: bearded tough man, cowboy hat, denim shirt, stern stare
scruffy tomcat, scared expression

wordplay.explanation: German 'Kater' means both 'hangover' and 'tomcat': Chuck has no hangover, the tomcat 'has' Chuck.

ru.note: No hangover/tomcat pun in Russian; use another Chuck Norris fact or a new pun.

en.note: No hangover/tomcat pun in English; replace with an English Chuck Norris fact pun.

gist: Man asks a Thai woman for her phone number; her accented English digits sound like an offer of free sex, until her boyfriend translates them back into numbers.

en.note: Pun is already in English; keep the digits as spoken.

en.note: Replace with an English fold pun, e.g. a refusal using 'fold' or 'paper-thin chance'.

en.note: Rebuild the mishearings with English sound-alikes; drop the dialect.
